items.title: Species are vanishing 100 to 1000 times faster than normal
items.claim: The fossil record gives a 'background' extinction rate: roughly 1 species per million per year. Current rates are 100 to 1000 times that — and rising. Many biologists call it the sixth mass extinction.

options.text: Asteroid impact like 66 million years ago
Habitat destruction (especially tropical deforestation), invasive species, climate change, pollution and overharvesting — a multi-cause anthropogenic mass extinction with no single dominant mechanism

items.reveal:
The five previous mass extinctions (Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous) each saw 50-95% of species disappear over geological timescales. The Permian was the worst — ~96% of marine species lost over ~60,000 years.

The current rate, calculated from documented vertebrate extinctions (Ceballos, Ehrlich and others), is 100-1000 times background. Insect biomass declines (Hallmann et al. 2017, Krefeld study) show 75% reductions over 27 years in German nature reserves.

Human impacts: forest cover reduced by ~30% globally since 1700; ocean fish biomass down ~50% since 1970; freshwater vertebrates down 84% (WWF Living Planet Report). Climate change adds an accelerating layer.

Protected areas and conservation work — by some measures, extinction rates would have been 4x higher without them.

Mass extinctions reshape evolution for tens of millions of years. We won't return to the world we know within human-relevant timeframes — the species we lose are lost.
items.why: Species loss feels gradual. The rate is geological in magnitude — comparable to events that left fossil-record-defining boundaries. We are living through one.

items.title: Plants and oceans cycle far more CO2 than humans release — yet we still drive the trend
items.claim: Humans emit ~10 gigatonnes of carbon per year. Natural fluxes (photosynthesis ~120 Gt, ocean exchange ~80 Gt, respiration ~120 Gt) dwarf this. Yet atmospheric CO2 keeps rising. The natural fluxes are roughly balanced — human emissions are a small but unmatched addition.
items.prompt: Why does a small flux dominate the trend?

options.text: The large natural fluxes are bidirectional and roughly balanced; the small human flux is NET addition. Imagine a bath whose inflow exactly equals outflow — a slow added trickle raises the water level whether the main flow is large or not
Plants absorb only certain types of CO2

items.reveal_title: Flux vs reservoir vs net change
items.reveal:
Reservoirs (rough sizes in gigatonnes of carbon):
Atmosphere: ~880 (and rising)
Oceans: ~38,000 (most as dissolved bicarbonate, slow exchange with deep ocean)
Soils: ~1,500-2,400
Vegetation: ~450-650
Fossil fuels: ~4,000+ (decreasing as we burn them)

Fluxes (Gt C per year):
Photosynthesis: ~120 (atmosphere to land)
Land respiration: ~120 (back to atmosphere)
Ocean uptake: ~80 (atmosphere to ocean)
Ocean release: ~78 (ocean to atmosphere)
Fossil emissions: ~10 (geological store to atmosphere)
Land-use change: ~1-2 net (mostly deforestation)

The natural fluxes are within ~1% of balance. The fossil flux is unbalanced — it's NET addition with no matching natural removal at the same scale. About half is absorbed by oceans and land 'sinks'; half stays airborne. Atmospheric CO2 rises ~2.5 ppm/year.

Residence time vs adjustment time: an individual CO2 molecule exchanges with the ocean in years. But removing the EXCESS takes much longer (hundreds to thousands of years for the surface ocean, ~100,000 years for full geological recovery).
items.why: The 'humans only emit 4% of CO2 turnover' argument confuses flux with net change. A small net addition into a near-balanced cycle is what matters, and it accumulates.

items.title: Octopuses change colour while being colour-blind
items.claim: Cephalopods produce sophisticated colour displays — mimicking corals, fish, sand — using chromatophore cells embedded in the skin. Their actual eyes have only one photoreceptor type. They cannot distinguish red from green.
items.prompt: How do octopuses match colour without seeing it?

options.text: They have hidden colour vision we haven't found
Their SKIN contains opsin proteins — the same light-sensitive receptors used in eyes — likely giving the surface itself wavelength-sensitivity that the eyes lack
Other octopuses signal the colour to them

items.reveal_title: Distributed colour vision via opsin-expressing skin
items.reveal:
Cephalopod skin expresses several genes (including r-opsin and rhodopsin-like proteins) usually found in eyes. Ramirez and Oakley (2015) showed Octopus bimaculoides skin responds to specific wavelengths.

The hypothesis: the chromatic information bypasses the brain entirely. The skin senses ambient colour and adjusts the chromatophore display locally without needing centralised colour vision.

It's also possible they exploit the chromatic aberration of their unusual U-shaped pupils to extract colour information from a single photoreceptor type — Stubbs and Stubbs (2016) — but the experimental support is mixed. Either way, cephalopod colour matching is a fascinating biological riddle.
items.why: Vision is assumed to happen in eyes and brains. In cephalopods it may happen distributed across the body.
